claims.text: Adding approximately 1 at% Y to a refractory high-entropy alloy promotes in-situ formation of nanoscale Y-oxide precipitates during controlled thermal treatment.
The resulting Y-oxide precipitates have low density.
Nanoscale Y-oxide precipitates pin grain boundaries.
The nanoprecipitates increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
The nanoprecipitates improve elevated-temperature creep resistance.
Y-oxide nanoparticles remain stable during elevated-temperature exposure.
The proposed strength and creep improvements hold between 900 and 1200 degrees Celsius.
Approximately 1 at% Y produces a statistically significant increase in high-temperature yield strength relative to the Y-free baseline.
Approximately 1 at% Y produces a statistically significant increase in creep resistance relative to the Y-free baseline.
The Y addition leaves room-temperature tensile ductility essentially unchanged.
The Y addition leaves room-temperature tensile strength essentially unchanged.
A low precipitate volume fraction and low precipitate density prevent degradation of the room-temperature ductile BCC matrix.
The NbMoCrTiAl-type baseline is a predominantly single-phase BCC solid solution with minimal or no precipitates.
Larger Y additions may adversely affect density or room-temperature mechanical performance.
Deviation from the optimized thermal cycle may adversely affect density or room-temperature mechanical performance.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as an untreated alloy, whereas the decisive experiment subjects both baseline and Y-modified alloys to the same thermal treatment. It is unclear whether 'untreated' means Y-free or not heat-treated, leaving the comparator inconsistently specified.
